name: Raymond Fletcher
presenting_complaint: Sudden severe generalised abdominal pain for 4 hours, now rigid and unwell

medications: Regular naproxen 500 mg twice daily for knee pain
medical_history.social: Ex-smoker (30 pack-years). Drinks 3-4 standard drinks most nights. Retired carpenter, lives with wife.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: Raymond Fletcher, a 67-year-old man, presents to ED with sudden-onset severe generalised abdominal pain that began 4 hours ago while at rest. The pain is constant, worse on any movement, and he is lying very still. He has taken regular naproxen for knee arthritis. He looks unwell, sweaty and grey. Obs: BP 94/58, HR 122, RR 26, temp 38.4, SpO2 95%. Abdomen is board-rigid with generalised guarding and absent bowel sounds.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: SOCRATES of pain: sudden-onset, generalised, constant severe pain, worse on movement, patient lies still (peritonitic pattern) - onset 4 hours ago
Risk factors for perforated viscus: chronic NSAID use (naproxen), previous peptic ulcer disease, alcohol, ex-smoker
Associated symptoms: nausea, vomiting, anorexia, fevers/rigors, last bowel motion and flatus, abdominal distension
Red-flag / must-not-miss screen: preceding dyspepsia or melaena, change in bowel habit or PR bleeding, prior diverticulitis, weight loss
Cardiovascular screen to exclude mimics: no tearing back pain (AAA/dissection), no ischaemic-type chest pain (inferior MI can present as epigastric pain)
Medication, anticoagulant, allergy history and fasting/last oral intake time for theatre
objective: Full set of vital signs and calculate a sepsis/early-warning score - recognise septic shock (hypotension + tachycardia + fever)
Abdominal exam: generalised rigidity, board-like abdomen, guarding, rebound/percussion tenderness, absent bowel sounds, loss of liver dullness
Assess for peritonism and haemodynamic instability; PR examination; check hernial orifices
Erect chest X-ray looking for free gas (air) under the diaphragm - can be obtained rapidly at the bedside
CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast is the definitive investigation to confirm perforation and identify source (arrange urgently once resuscitation started)
VBG with lactate at the bedside to quantify tissue hypoperfusion; bedside ECG to exclude inferior MI mimic
assessment: Perforated intra-abdominal viscus with generalised peritonitis - most likely perforated peptic ulcer given NSAID use and prior PUD (differential: perforated diverticulum/colon, perforated appendix)
Septic shock / sepsis secondary to intra-abdominal source (hypotensive, tachycardic, febrile, raised lactate expected)
Consider and exclude mimics of the acute abdomen: ruptured/leaking AAA, acute mesenteric ischaemia, inferior myocardial infarction, acute pancreatitis
plan: Call the surgical registrar EARLY - this is a theatre decision for emergency laparotomy, not a medical problem (FIRST action)
A to E resuscitation: two large-bore IV cannulae, IV fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloid boluses (e.g. 500 mL Hartmann's/Plasma-Lyte, reassess) for hypotension
Keep strictly nil by mouth; insert nasogastric tube on free drainage for gastric decompression

IV antibiotics for intra-abdominal sepsis WITHIN 1 hour (eTG): amoxicillin/ampicillin 2 g IV + gentamicin IV (e.g. 5-7 mg/kg) + metronidazole 500 mg IV; piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV is an alternative single agent
Adequate IV analgesia titrated to effect (e.g. fentanyl 25-50 microg IV or morphine 2.5-5 mg IV titrated) plus antiemetic (ondansetron 4 mg IV) - do NOT withhold analgesia to 'avoid masking signs'
Bloods: VBG/lactate, FBC, UEC, LFT, lipase, coags, CRP, BSL and GROUP AND HOLD/crossmatch; blood cultures before antibiotics if it does not delay them
Indwelling urinary catheter and strict fluid balance; monitor urine output as marker of resuscitation; erect CXR then urgent CT abdomen/pelvis
Consent and prepare for emergency laparotomy: fasting, IV fluids, VTE assessment, inform anaesthetics/theatre, escalate to consultant; admit under surgical unit

critical_errors: Discharging the patient, or delaying/not arranging urgent surgical review - a septic patient with a rigid peritonitic abdomen needs an emergency surgical assessment for theatre, not observation at home
Allowing oral intake (food or fluids) in a patient likely heading to emergency laparotomy - must be kept strictly nil by mouth
Withholding or significantly delaying IV antibiotics in a septic peritonitic patient (e.g. waiting for the CT before giving antibiotics)
must_not_miss: Perforated viscus with generalised peritonitis requiring emergency laparotomy
Sepsis / septic shock treated with early IV antibiotics and fluid resuscitation (Sepsis Six)
Early surgical registrar referral for a theatre decision
Ruptured/leaking AAA and inferior MI considered and excluded as mimics
